questions.question: Which of the following aqueous solutions will have the maximum boiling point?
What will be the molarity of 30 ml of 0.5 M H$_2$SO$_4$ solution diluted to 50 ml?
questions.answer:
**(A)** 0.3 M

Dilution changes the volume but not the number of moles, so $M_1V_1=M_2V_2$:

$$M_2=\frac{M_1V_1}{V_2}=\frac{0.5\times30}{50}=0.3\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**0.3 M.** The solution is diluted 30/50 = 0.6 times, so the concentration falls by the same factor.

questions.question: A plant cell shrinks when it is kept in a
questions.answer:
**(B)** Hypertonic solution

In a **hypertonic** solution the solute concentration outside is **greater** than inside the cell, so water leaves the cell by osmosis across the semi-permeable membrane. The protoplasm loses water and pulls away from the cell wall — the cell shrinks (plasmolysis). In a hypotonic solution water enters and the cell becomes turgid; in pure water the effect is strongest of all. This is why salting or sugaring preserves food: it creates a hypertonic medium that dehydrates microbial cells.

questions.question: The amount of electricity required to obtain 1 mol of Cu from CuSO$_4$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** 2 F

$$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- -> Cu}$$

Copper is deposited from CuSO$_4$ as Cu(II), which needs **two electrons per ion** — so two moles of electrons, i.e. **2 faraday** (2 × 96500 = 193000 C), deposit one mole (63.5 g) of copper. One faraday would give only half a mole.

questions.question: The cell which is used in automobiles and inverters are
questions.answer:
**(A)** Lead storage battery

The **lead–acid accumulator** is the secondary cell used in cars and inverters. Its electrodes are lead and lead dioxide in dilute sulphuric acid:

$$\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 <=> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}$$

It delivers a large current for a short time (exactly what a starter motor needs) and can be **recharged** many times. The nickel–cadmium cell is rechargeable but is used in portable appliances, and the dry cell and fuel cell are not used as automotive storage batteries.

questions.question: Calculate the overall order of a reaction which has the rate expression: Rate = k[A]$^{1/2}$[B]$^{3/2}$
questions.answer:
**(A)** Second order

The overall order is the sum of the exponents:

$$\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{4}{2}=2$$

So the reaction is **second order overall**, though it is half-order in A and three-halves order in B — a reminder that order can be fractional even when the total is integral.

questions.question: Activation energy of a chemical reaction can be determined by
options: rate constants at two different temperatures
orientation of reactant molecules during the collision
questions.answer:
**(B)** rate constants at two different temperatures

From the Arrhenius equation,

$$\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{T_2-T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$$

so measuring the rate constant at **two temperatures** allows $E_a$ to be calculated. (Equivalently, the slope of a plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ is $-E_a/2.303R$.) A single rate constant at one temperature gives only the product $Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, from which $E_a$ cannot be separated. Orientation and catalysts affect the rate but are not ways of *measuring* the activation energy.

questions.question: For a first order reaction the correct graph is (a plot of ln[R$_0$] against time t)
questions.answer:
**(B)** ln[R$_0$] vs time, K = −slope

For a first-order reaction,

$$\ln[\ce{R_0}]=-kt+\ln[\ce{R_0}]_0$$

So a plot of **$\ln[\ce{R_0}]$ against time is a straight line** of **slope $-k$** and intercept $\ln[\ce{R_0}]_0$. A plot of concentration itself against time is exponential, and $\log[\ce{R}]$ against $t$ also gives a straight line but with slope $-k/2.303$, so the graph must be the natural-log plot to read $k$ directly.

questions.question: A transition element X is placed in the first series of transition elements. It has the following characteristics: (i) It is a coinage metal. (ii) It has positive reduction potential. (iii) It does not react with HCl but reacts with nitric acid. The element X is likely to be
questions.answer:
**(B)** Cu

Copper fits all three clues:

- **(i)** It is a **coinage metal** (Cu, Ag, Au).
- **(ii)** $E^\circ_{\ce{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}=+0.34$ V — **positive**, so it is not displaced by hydrogen and is noble towards non-oxidising acids. (Zn has −0.76 V, strongly negative.)
- **(iii)** It does **not** react with HCl (H$^+$ cannot oxidise it), but it **does** dissolve in nitric acid, which acts as an oxidising agent:

$$\ce{3Cu + 8HNO3(dil) -> 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O}$$

Moreover it is a **first-series** (3d) element, which rules out Ag and Au (both 4d/5d).

questions.question: Which of the following oxidation states is common for all lanthanoids?
questions.answer:
**(B)** +3

**All lanthanoids show the +3 oxidation state**, formed by loss of the two 6s electrons and one 4f electron. It is the most stable state for every member of the series, which is why their chemistry is so uniform and their separation so difficult.

The +2 and +4 states occur only where a stable $f^0$, $f^7$ or $f^{14}$ configuration can be reached (Ce$^{4+}$, $f^0$; Eu$^{2+}$, $f^7$; Yb$^{2+}$, $f^{14}$), and **+5 does not occur at all** for lanthanoids — that is characteristic of the actinoids (e.g. Pa(V), Np(V)).

questions.question: Identify the homoleptic complex among the following compounds
questions.answer:
**(B)** [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$

A **homoleptic** complex contains only **one kind of ligand**. $[\ce{Ni(CN)4}]^{2-}$ has four cyanide ligands and nothing else, so it is homoleptic — and it is square planar and diamagnetic ($dsp^2$).

The others are heteroleptic: $[\ce{Co(NH3)4Cl2}]^+$ mixes ammine with chloride, and $[\ce{Cr(NH3)2Cl2(en)}]^+$ mixes ammine, chloride and ethylenediamine.

questions.question: Which of the following is a bidentate ligand?
questions.answer:
**(C)** C$_2$O$_4^{2-}$

The **oxalate ion** has two carboxylate oxygens, each with a lone pair, and can bind the metal through **both at once**, forming a five-membered chelate ring — so it is **bidentate**. Cyanide, ammonia and carbonate each donate through a single atom (carbonate is normally monodentate), so they are monodentate ligands.

questions.question: S$_N$1 reaction will be fastest in case of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Tertiary halide

An S$_N$1 reaction proceeds through a **carbocation intermediate**, so its rate is governed by carbocation stability. A **tertiary** halide gives a 3° carbocation, stabilised by hyperconjugation and inductive donation from three alkyl groups, so it ionises fastest:

$$\ce{R3C-X -> R3C^+ + X^-}\quad(\text{slow, rate-determining})$$

The order is **tertiary > secondary > primary** — exactly the reverse of S$_N$2, where steric hindrance makes the primary halide fastest.

questions.question: The best method for the synthesis of alkyl fluoride is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Swarts reaction

Alkyl fluorides cannot be made by the usual halide-exchange route because F$^-$ is a poor nucleophile in protic media. In the **Swarts reaction** an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a **metallic fluoride** — AgF, Hg$_2$F$_2$ or CoF$_3$:

$$\ce{CH3Br + AgF -> CH3F + AgBr}$$

The metal fluoride provides a strongly polarised fluorine and the precipitation of the silver halide drives the exchange. (Finkelstein is for iodides, Kolbe for hydrocarbons, Wurtz for coupling.)

questions.question: $\ce{CH3CH=CH2 ->[H^+/H2O]}$ A. Major product is
questions.answer:
**(B)** CH$_3$CH(OH)CH$_3$

Acid-catalysed hydration of propene follows **Markovnikov's rule**: the proton adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable **secondary carbocation**, which water then attacks:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H^+ -> CH3-C^+H-CH3 ->[H2O] CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}$$

The major product is **propan-2-ol**. Propan-1-ol would require anti-Markovnikov addition (hydroboration–oxidation, $\ce{BH3}$ then $\ce{H2O2/OH^-}$).

questions.question: IUPAC name of ethoxybenzene is
questions.answer:
**(C)** Ethoxybenzene

$\ce{C6H5-O-C2H5}$ is named with the benzene ring as the parent (benzene) and the ether group as an **alkoxy substituent**: **ethoxybenzene** (trivial name: phenetole).

Naming it 'ethoxide' would describe the anion $\ce{C2H5O^-}$, and 'benzyl' implies a $\ce{C6H5CH2-}$ group, which is not present — so only ethoxybenzene is correct.

questions.question: CH$_3$CH$_2$O$^-$Na$^+$ + CH$_3$Cl → P. Product 'P' is
questions.answer:
**(B)** CH$_3$CH$_2$OCH$_3$

The alkoxide ion is a nucleophile and displaces chloride from the methyl halide in an S$_N$2 reaction (**Williamson synthesis**):

$$\ce{C2H5O^-Na^+ + CH3Cl -> C2H5-O-CH3 + NaCl}$$

The product is **methoxyethane** (ethyl methyl ether) — an unsymmetrical ether, which is exactly what the Williamson method allows. Elimination to ethene would need a strong base and a secondary/tertiary halide.

questions.question: Tollens' reagent is used to distinguish between
questions.answer:
**(B)** Aldehydes and ketones

**Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal silver nitrate, containing $[\ce{Ag(NH3)2}]^+$) is a mild oxidising agent. An **aldehyde** reduces it to metallic silver, giving a bright silver mirror:

$$\ce{RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]^+ + 3OH^- -> RCOO^- + 2Ag v + 4NH3 + 2H2O}$$

A **ketone** has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and does not react, so the test cleanly distinguishes the two. (Amines are distinguished by Hinsberg's reagent; acids by NaHCO$_3$.)

questions.question: In Clemmensen reduction, carbonyl compound is reduced in the presence of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zn—Hg + HCl

The **Clemmensen reduction** uses **zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid** to convert an aldehyde or ketone to the alkane:

$$\ce{R-CO-R' ->[Zn(Hg)][conc. HCl] R-CH2-R'}$$

The strongly acidic medium is why it complements the Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine + KOH). Sodium in ethanol is a milder reductant (Bouveault–Blanc, for esters) and sodium in dry ether is the Wurtz coupling reagent.

questions.question: Identify the Hinsberg reagent:
questions.answer:
**(C)** C$_6$H$_5$SO$_2$Cl

**Hinsberg's reagent** is **benzenesulphonyl chloride, $\ce{C6H5SO2Cl}$**. It reacts with 1° and 2° amines to give sulphonamides that differ in their solubility in alkali — the 1° amine product still has an H on nitrogen and so is acidic and dissolves in KOH, while the 2° amine product does not. A 3° amine has no H on nitrogen and does not react at all:

$$\ce{C6H5SO2Cl + RNH2 -> C6H5SO2NHR + HCl}$$

Benzamide and benzoyl chloride are acid-derivatives, not the Hinsberg reagent.

questions.question: Which one of the following reactions will not form primary amine?
questions.answer:
**(C)** CH$_3$NC + LiAlH$_4$

(A) is the **Hofmann bromamide** degradation (amide → amine with one carbon less) giving methylamine; (B) reduces the nitrile to ethylamine; (D) reduces the amide to propylamine — all **primary** amines.

A **methyl isocyanide**, however, is $\ce{CH3-N#C}$, with the carbon attached to nitrogen; reduction gives $\ce{CH3-NH-CH3}$ — **dimethylamine, a secondary amine** (via N-methylformaldimine). So (C) is the one that does not give a primary amine.

questions.question: Which of the following is an Aldohexose?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Glucose

**Glucose** is an **aldohexose** — six carbons with an aldehyde group at C-1: $\ce{CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CHO}$. Cellulose is a polysaccharide (a polymer of glucose), sucrose is a disaccharide and raffinose a trisaccharide, so none of them is a monosaccharide at all.

questions.question: An example of fibrous protein is
questions.answer:
**(C)** Both (A) and (B)

**Keratin** (hair, wool, nails, horn) and **myosin** (the contractile protein of muscle) are both **fibrous proteins**: their polypeptide chains lie side by side in long threads, held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, they are insoluble in water and they play structural/contractile roles.

*Note on the printed key:* the paper ticks (A) and (C). Keratin alone is not the complete answer — myosin is equally a fibrous protein, so (C) is correct.

questions.question: α-helix structure is found in
questions.answer:
**(D)** Protein

The **$\alpha$-helix** is a **secondary structure of proteins**: the polypeptide backbone coils into a right-handed helix with about 3.6 amino-acid residues per turn, held by **hydrogen bonds between the $\ce{C=O}$ of one residue and the $\ce{N-H}$ of the fourth residue along the chain** (intra-chain). DNA and RNA have their own helical structures (the double helix and various RNA helices), while lipids are not polymers of amino acids.

questions.question: Vitamin C is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Water soluble

**Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** is **water-soluble**, like the B-group vitamins; it is not stored in the body to any extent and excess is excreted in urine, so a regular dietary supply is needed and an overdose is not toxic. Deficiency causes **scurvy**. Vitamins A, D, E and K, by contrast, are fat-soluble and stored in the liver, so an excess can be harmful.

questions.question: Define mole fraction.
questions.answer:
**Mole fraction** of a component in a mixture is the ratio of the number of moles of that component to the **total number of moles of all components** present:

$$x_A=\frac{n_A}{n_A+n_B},\qquad x_B=\frac{n_B}{n_A+n_B}$$

It is dimensionless and the sum of all mole fractions in a mixture is 1. For a solution of a non-volatile solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute:

$$\frac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=x_2$$

Unlike molarity, mole fraction does not change with temperature.

questions.question: Calculate the half-life period of a first order reaction whose rate constant is 200 s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
For a first-order reaction,

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

With $k=200\ \text{s}^{-1}$:

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{200}=3.47\times10^{-3}\ \text{s}$$

**The half-life is about 3.5 x 10$^{-3}$ s (3.47 ms).** The reaction is extremely fast, and $t_{1/2}$ is independent of the initial concentration - the defining property of first-order kinetics.

questions.question: Why is Zn not considered as transition element? (Z = 30)
Draw the structure of geometrical isomers of [Co(NH$_3$)$_4$Cl$_2$]$^+$.
questions.answer:
$[\ce{Co(NH3)4Cl2}]^+$ is an octahedral $\ce{MA4B2}$ complex, and it exists as **two geometrical isomers**:

**(i) cis-isomer** — the two Cl ligands occupy **adjacent** (90°) positions; the four NH$_3$ are then arranged as two pairs, one NH$_3$ being trans to each Cl. This isomer is **polar** (has a net dipole) and is violet.

**(ii) trans-isomer** — the two Cl ligands occupy **opposite** ends of an axis (180°), with all four NH$_3$ lying in the equatorial plane. This isomer is **non-polar** by symmetry and is green.

The two differ in colour, dipole moment and solubility. There are no optical isomers, because neither structure is chiral.

questions.question: Identify X and Y in the following reaction: bromobenzene $\xrightarrow{Mg/\text{dry ether}}$ X $\xrightarrow{H_2O}$ Y + Mg(OH)Br
questions.answer:
**X is phenylmagnesium bromide, $\ce{C6H5MgBr}$** — the Grignard reagent formed when bromobenzene reacts with magnesium in dry ether:

$$\ce{C6H5Br + Mg ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5MgBr}$$

**Y is benzene, $\ce{C6H6}$.** Water hydrolyses the Grignard reagent, the carbanion picking up a proton:

$$\ce{C6H5MgBr + H2O -> C6H6 + Mg(OH)Br}$$

This hydrolysis is why the ether must be strictly dry and why Grignard reagents are destroyed by moisture. (With D$_2$O the product would be $\ce{C6H5D}$, which is how the mechanism was proved.)

questions.question: Alcohols are more soluble in water than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular masses. Why?
questions.answer:
Because an alcohol can form **hydrogen bonds with water**, whereas a hydrocarbon cannot.

The $\ce{-OH}$ group of the alcohol has a hydrogen attached to a small, strongly electronegative oxygen (so the H is $\delta+$) and a lone pair on the oxygen (so the O is $\delta-$). Water, $\ce{H-O-H}$, can both donate a hydrogen bond to the alcohol's oxygen and accept one from its $\ce{O-H}$. These solute–solvent hydrogen bonds release energy that compensates for the breaking of water–water hydrogen bonds, so the alcohol dissolves readily.

A hydrocarbon has only C–H bonds, which are almost non-polar, so it can form only weak London dispersion forces with water; the water–water hydrogen bonds are not compensated, and the hydrocarbon is essentially insoluble. That is also why solubility falls as the alkyl chain lengthens (methanol and ethanol are fully miscible; octanol is barely soluble).

questions.question: Write the IUPAC name of (CH$_3$)$_3$CNH$_2$.
questions.answer:
**2-methylpropan-2-amine** (trivial name: *tert*-butylamine).

The longest chain containing the carbon attached to nitrogen has three carbons, $\ce{C-C(NH2)-C}$, and numbering from that carbon gives the amino group locant 1 — but the two methyls on C-2 are better treated by choosing the parent as propane with the $\ce{-NH2}$ and a methyl both on C-2:

$$\ce{(CH3)3C-NH2}$$

So the parent is propan-2-amine with a methyl at C-2: **2-methylpropan-2-amine**. It is a primary amine, and being tertiary at the $\alpha$-carbon it cannot be made by the Gabriel synthesis but is prepared from *tert*-butyl chloride by the Hofmann route.

questions.question: Name the reaction in which aldehydes with no α-hydrogen atom undergo self-oxidation and reduction in presence of conc. alkali.
questions.answer:
**Cannizzaro reaction.**

An aldehyde with **no $\alpha$-hydrogen** (e.g. formaldehyde, benzaldehyde) undergoes **disproportionation** in concentrated alkali — one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate salt and another is reduced to the alcohol:

$$\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$$

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + NaOH -> C6H5COONa + C6H5CH2OH}$$

A hydride ion is transferred from the hydrate anion of one molecule to the carbonyl carbon of the other. Because there is no $\alpha$-H, the competing aldol condensation cannot occur, so disproportionation is the only pathway.

questions.question: Write the name of any one source of vitamin A.
questions.answer:
**Fish-liver oil (cod-liver oil)** — the richest natural source of preformed **retinol**. Other sources are liver, butter, egg yolk, milk and cheese; and **carrots, green leafy vegetables and yellow fruits** supply **$\beta$-carotene**, which the body converts into vitamin A.

Vitamin A is needed for the visual pigment rhodopsin (deficiency causes night blindness) and for healthy epithelia and growth.

questions.question: State Kohlrausch's law. Calculate $\Lambda^\circ_m$ for Cl$^-$ ion from the data given below: $\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{MgCl2})=258.6$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$; $\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{Mg^{2+}})=106.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
**Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:** at infinite dilution, when dissociation is complete, each ion migrates independently of its co-ion, and the **molar conductivity of an electrolyte at infinite dilution is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its constituent ions**, each multiplied by its number in the formula:

$$\Lambda^\circ_m=\nu_+\lambda^\circ_+ + \nu_-\lambda^\circ_-$$

For magnesium chloride:

$$\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{MgCl2})=\lambda^\circ(\ce{Mg^{2+}})+2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl^-})$$

$$258.6=106.0+2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl^-})$$

$$2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl^-})=152.6\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl^-})=76.3\ \text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$$

**The limiting molar conductivity of the chloride ion is 76.3 S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.**

The law is what makes it possible to obtain $\Lambda^\circ_m$ for a weak electrolyte such as acetic acid, by combining the values for strong electrolytes:

$$\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{CH3COOH})=\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{CH3COONa})+\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{HCl})-\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{NaCl})$$

questions.question: Calculate the magnetic moment of the following ions: (a) Ti$^{2+}$ (Z = 22) (b) Zn$^{2+}$ (Z = 30) (c) Cr$^{2+}$ (Z = 24)
questions.answer:
The spin-only moments are $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ B.M.

**(a) Ti$^{2+}$:** Ti is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^24s^2$, so Ti$^{2+}$ is $3d^2$ — two unpaired electrons:

$$\mu=\sqrt{2(2+2)}=\sqrt{8}=2.83\ \text{B.M.}$$

**(b) Zn$^{2+}$:** $3d^{10}$ — all electrons paired, so $n=0$:

$$\mu=0\ \text{B.M.}\quad(\text{diamagnetic})$$

**(c) Cr$^{2+}$:** Cr is $[\ce{Ar}]3d^54s^1$, so Cr$^{2+}$ is $3d^4$ — four unpaired electrons:

$$\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24}=4.90\ \text{B.M.}$$

**Ti$^{2+}$ 2.83 B.M., Zn$^{2+}$ 0 (diamagnetic), Cr$^{2+}$ 4.90 B.M.**

questions.question: Write the steps for the preparation of potassium dichromate (K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$) from chromite ore.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — oxidation of chromite to chromate.** Powdered chromite ore, $\ce{FeCr2O4}$ (Cr in +3), is fused with sodium carbonate in a plentiful supply of air:

$$\ce{4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2}$$

Chromium is oxidised from +3 to +6; the yellow solution of sodium chromate is filtered off from the iron(III) oxide. (With NaOH: $\ce{4FeCr2O4 + 16NaOH + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8H2O}$.)

**Step 2 — acidification to dichromate.** The filtrate is acidified with sulphuric acid; the chromate is converted to the dichromate, which is stable only in acid and is orange:

$$\ce{2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O}$$

**Step 3 — conversion to the potassium salt.** Potassium chloride is added and the mixture cooled; **potassium dichromate is less soluble** than the sodium salt, so it crystallises out:

$$\ce{Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl -> K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl}$$

The orange-red crystals are filtered, recrystallised from water and dried.

questions.question: Write the formulae of the following coordination compounds: (a) Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride (b) Potassium trioxalatoaluminate(III) (c) Tetrahydroxozincate(II)
questions.answer:
**(a) Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride:** four NH$_3$, one H$_2$O, one Cl$^-$ on Co(III); the complex ion has charge $+3+0+0+(-1)=+2$, so two chlorides balance it:

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)4(H2O)Cl]Cl2}$$

**(b) Potassium trioxalatoaluminate(III):** Al(III) with three bidentate oxalates gives $+3+3(-2)=-3$, so three K$^+$:

$$\ce{K3[Al(C2O4)3]}$$

**(c) Tetrahydroxozincate(II):** Zn(II) with four OH$^-$ gives $+2+4(-1)=-2$:

$$\ce{[Zn(OH)4]^{2-}}$$

(isolated as the salt $\ce{Na2[Zn(OH)4]}$, formed when zinc dissolves in excess alkali).

questions.question: Predict the product: (a) $\ce{C6H5OH ->[Zn dust][\Delta]}$ (b) anisole $\xrightarrow[\mathrm{conc.\ H2SO4}]{concat\ HNO3}$ (c) $\ce{CH3COOH ->[\text{(i) red P/Cl2}][\text{(ii) }H2O]}$
questions.answer:
**(a) Phenol with zinc dust on heating** is reduced to **benzene** — the standard laboratory method for removing the hydroxyl group:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + Zn ->[\Delta] C6H6 + ZnO}$$

**(b) Anisole with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids:** the $\ce{-OCH3}$ group is activating and **ortho/para directing**, so nitration gives mainly the para product because the methoxy group is bulky:

$$\ce{C6H5OCH3 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4] p-NO2C6H4OCH3 + o-NO2C6H4OCH3 + H2O}$$

**p-Nitroanisole** is the major product (plus some o-nitroanisole).

**(c) Acetic acid with red phosphorus and chlorine, then water — the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction:** the acid is converted to its acid chloride and brominated/chlorinated at the $\alpha$-carbon; hydrolysis gives the **$\alpha$-chloro acid**:

$$\ce{CH3COOH ->[Cl2/P] ClCH2COCl ->[H2O] ClCH2COOH}$$

The product is **chloroacetic acid** (2-chloroethanoic acid), a much stronger acid than acetic acid because the electronegative chlorine stabilises the carboxylate ion.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following conversions? (a) Butan-2-ol to Butan-2-one (b) Chloromethane to ethane (c) Benzoyl chloride to benzaldehyde
questions.answer:
**(a) Butan-2-ol → butan-2-one:** oxidation of the secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate (or CrO$_3$, Jones reagent):

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 ->[K2Cr2O7][H2SO4] CH3CH2COCH3 + H2O}$$

**(b) Chloromethane → ethane:** coupling with sodium in dry ether, the **Wurtz reaction**:

$$\ce{2CH3Cl + 2Na ->[\text{dry ether}] CH3-CH3 + 2NaCl}$$

**(c) Benzoyl chloride → benzaldehyde:** catalytic hydrogenation over a **poisoned palladium catalyst** — the **Rosenmund reduction**:

$$\ce{C6H5COCl + H2 ->[Pd/BaSO4] C6H5CHO + HCl}$$

Boiling the Pd/BaSO$_4$ with a little sulphur or quinoline poisons it just enough to stop the reduction at the aldehyde stage; without the poison the product would be reduced further to benzyl alcohol.

questions.question: Write the hydrolysis products of the following: (a) lactose (b) sucrose (c) maltose
questions.answer:
**(a) Lactose** — a disaccharide of $\beta$-D-galactose and D-glucose linked $\beta$-1,4. Hydrolysis gives **galactose and glucose**:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{lactase}] C6H12O6(\text{galactose}) + C6H12O6(\text{glucose})}$$

**(b) Sucrose** — $\alpha$-D-glucose linked 1,2 to $\beta$-D-fructose. Hydrolysis (by the enzyme **invertase**) gives **glucose and fructose**, an equimolar mixture called *invert sugar* because the rotation changes from dextro to laevo:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{invertase}] C6H12O6(\text{glucose}) + C6H12O6(\text{fructose})}$$

**(c) Maltose** — two glucose units joined $\alpha$-1,4 (malt sugar). Hydrolysis gives **two molecules of glucose**:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{maltase}] 2C6H12O6}$$

Lactose and maltose are **reducing** sugars; sucrose is **non-reducing**, because both its anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond.

questions.question: Write the IUPAC names of the following: (a) Ph—CH=CH—CHO (b) CH$_3$—C(Cl)(CH$_3$)—CH$_2$Br (c) 2-acetylcyclohexan-1-ol
questions.answer:
**(a) $\ce{Ph-CH=CH-CHO}$** — a three-carbon aldehyde chain with a phenyl at C-3 and a double bond between C-2 and C-3, numbered from the aldehyde:

**3-phenylprop-2-enal** (cinnamaldehyde; the aldehyde responsible for the smell of cinnamon).

**(b) $\ce{CH3-C(Cl)(CH3)-CH2Br}$** — the longest chain is three carbons; numbering must give the two halogen-bearing carbons the lowest locants (1 and 2):

$$\ce{BrCH2-C(Cl)(CH3)-CH3}$$

**1-bromo-2-chloro-2-methylpropane**

**(c) A cyclohexane ring carrying an $\ce{-OH}$ and a $\ce{-COCH3}$ (acetyl) group on adjacent carbons** is named as an acetyl-substituted cyclohexanol with the alcohol as the principal functional group:

**2-acetylcyclohexan-1-ol**

(the $-\ce{OH}$ takes priority over the ketone for the suffix, so the ring is numbered from the carbon bearing it).

questions.question: Concentrated nitric acid used in laboratory work is 68% nitric acid by mass in aqueous solution. What should be the molarity of such a sample of the acid if the density of the solution is 1.540 g ml$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
Take **100 g of solution** (the mass percentage is independent of the amount chosen).

**Mass and moles of HNO$_3$:**

$$w=68\ \text{g},\qquad M(\ce{HNO3})=1+14+48=63\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

$$n=\frac{68}{63}=1.079\ \text{mol}$$

**Volume of that 100 g of solution:**

$$V=\frac{m}{\rho}=\frac{100}{1.540}=64.94\ \text{mL}=0.06494\ \text{L}$$

**Molarity:**

$$M=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{1.079}{0.06494}=16.62\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**The molarity is about 16.6 M** (≈16.7 M if the moles are taken as 68/63.01).

This very high value is typical of a concentrated strong acid: the solution is nearly 17 molar because a large mass of acid is packed into a small volume, and the density is greater than that of water. **Molality**, by contrast, would be $\dfrac{1.079}{0.032\ \text{kg}}=33.7$ m, since only 32 g of water is present — a good illustration of why molarity and molality diverge so much in concentrated solutions.

questions.question: Define electromotive force (EMF). Calculate the emf of the following cell: Zn(s) | Zn$^{2+}$(0.1 M) || Ag$^+$(0.01 M) | Ag(s). Given $E^\circ_{\ce{Zn^{2+}/Zn}}=-0.76$ V, $E^\circ_{\ce{Ag^+/Ag}}=+0.80$ V
questions.answer:
**Electromotive force (emf)** of a cell is the **maximum potential difference between its two electrodes when no current is drawn from the cell** — i.e. the cell potential measured under reversible conditions (open circuit). It is the difference of the electrode potentials,

$$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cathode}}-E_{\text{anode}}$$

and is related to the free energy change by $\Delta G=-nFE_{\text{cell}}$. It is measured in volts, and a positive emf means the cell reaction is spontaneous.

**Standard emf of this cell.** Zinc (more negative potential) is the anode, silver the cathode:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}=0.80-(-0.76)=+1.56\ \text{V}$$

The cell reaction is

$$\ce{Zn(s) + 2Ag^+ -> Zn^{2+} + 2Ag(s)},\qquad n=2$$

**Applying the Nernst equation:**

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{[\ce{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\ce{Ag^+}]^2}$$

$$\frac{0.1}{(0.01)^2}=\frac{0.1}{10^{-4}}=10^{3},\qquad \log10^{3}=3$$

$$E=1.56-\frac{0.0591}{2}\times3=1.56-0.02955\times3=1.56-0.0887$$

$$E=+1.47\ \text{V}$$

**The emf of the cell is 1.47 V.**

It is slightly **less** than the standard value because the anode ion is more concentrated than 1 M and the cathode ion much more dilute than 1 M — both changes oppose the forward reaction, in agreement with Le Chatelier's principle.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between order and molecularity. (b) Mention the factors that affect the rate of the chemical reactions.
questions.answer:
**(a) Order vs molecularity.**

| Order | Molecularity |
|---|---|
| Sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the **experimentally determined rate law** | Number of reacting species that collide simultaneously in an **elementary step** |
| Found **experimentally** | Derived from the **mechanism** — a theoretical concept |
| May be **zero, integral or fractional** | Always a **whole number** (1, 2, 3) |
| Applies to complex reactions as well as elementary ones | Applies only to elementary steps |
| Can be zero | Cannot be zero |

**(b) Factors affecting the rate.**

1. **Concentration of the reactants** — a higher concentration means a higher collision frequency, so a higher rate (rate $=k[\ce{A}]^n$). For solids, the **surface area** plays the same role: powder reacts faster than a lump.
2. **Temperature** — the rate rises steeply, roughly doubling or tripling per 10 K, because the fraction of molecules with energy above $E_a$ increases exponentially ($k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$).
3. **Catalyst** — provides an alternative path of lower activation energy, so the rate increases without the catalyst being consumed (and without changing the position of equilibrium).
4. **Nature and state of the reactants** — ionic reactions in solution are fast, covalent bond-breaking reactions slow; gases react faster than liquids or solids.
5. **Presence and intensity of light** — for photochemical reactions such as $\ce{H2 + Cl2 ->[h\nu] 2HCl}$, the rate depends on the intensity of radiation absorbed.
6. **Pressure** (for gaseous reactions) — equivalent to changing the concentration.

questions.question: [Fe(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{3+}$ is strongly paramagnetic whereas [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{3-}$ is weakly paramagnetic. Explain.
questions.answer:
Both complexes contain **Fe(III)**, which has the configuration $3d^5$. The difference lies entirely in the **strength of the ligand field**, which decides whether the five d electrons stay unpaired or pair up.

**$[\ce{Fe(H2O)6}]^{3+}$ — high spin (outer orbital).** Water is a **weak-field** ligand, so $\Delta_o$ is small and the electrons occupy all five d orbitals singly rather than pairing up:

$$3d: \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$$

With **five unpaired electrons** the complex is **strongly paramagnetic**:

$$\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35}=5.92\ \text{B.M.}$$

Because the 3d electrons are not re-organised, hybridisation uses the outer 4d orbitals ($sp^3d^2$), so it is an **outer-orbital (high-spin)** complex.

**$[\ce{Fe(CN)6}]^{3-}$ — low spin (inner orbital).** Cyanide is a **strong-field** ligand, so $\Delta_o$ is large and four of the five electrons pair up in the lower $t_{2g}$ set, leaving **one unpaired electron**:

$$3d: \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \ \_\ \ \_$$

$$\mu=\sqrt{1(1+2)}=\sqrt{3}=1.73\ \text{B.M.}$$

This is **weakly paramagnetic**. Pairing frees two 3d orbitals, so hybridisation is $d^2sp^3$ — an **inner-orbital (low-spin)** complex.

**Conclusion:** the magnetic moments (5.9 vs 1.7 B.M.) directly measure the number of unpaired electrons and therefore reveal the ligand-field strength: H$_2$O is weak-field, CN$^-$ strong-field. Both complexes are octahedral; the strong field also makes the cyanide complex low-spin and shifts its colour, and it is kinetically far more inert.

questions.question: Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) 3-bromo-2-methylpropene (b) m-nitrobenzoic acid (c) 4-bromoanisole (d) 3-chloro-4-phenylpentanoic acid (e) Picric acid
questions.answer:
**(a) 3-Bromo-2-methylpropene** — a three-carbon chain with a double bond between C-1 and C-2, a methyl on C-2 and bromine on C-3:

$$\ce{CH2=C(CH3)-CH2Br}$$

**(b) m-Nitrobenzoic acid** — benzoic acid with the $\ce{-NO2}$ at the meta position (C-3) relative to $\ce{-COOH}$:

$$\ce{3-NO2C6H4COOH}$$

**(c) 4-Bromoanisole** — anisole (methoxybenzene) with bromine at the position para to the methoxy group:

$$\ce{p-BrC6H4OCH3}$$

**(d) 3-Chloro-4-phenylpentanoic acid** — a five-carbon acid with Cl at C-3 and a phenyl at C-4:

$$\ce{HOOC-CH2-CH(Cl)-CH(C6H5)-CH3}$$

**(e) Picric acid** — 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: a benzene ring with $\ce{-OH}$ at C-1 and $\ce{-NO2}$ groups at C-2, C-4 and C-6:

$$\ce{2,4,6-(NO2)3C6H2OH}$$

It is made by nitrating phenol; despite being a phenol it is strongly acidic ($\text{p}K_a\approx0.4$) because the three nitro groups withdraw electron density and stabilise the phenoxide ion. (The name comes from its bitter taste and its use as a yellow dye/explosive.)

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Sandmeyer's reaction (b) Reimer-Tiemann reaction (c) Finkelstein reaction
questions.answer:
**(a) Sandmeyer's reaction.** A benzene diazonium salt is treated with a **copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid**, and the diazonium group is replaced by the halogen:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Br^- + CuBr/HBr -> C6H5Br + N2 ^ + CuBr2}$$

With CuCN/KCN the product is benzonitrile. It is the standard route from a primary aromatic amine to an aryl halide — a compound that cannot be made by direct halogenation when the substituent is deactivating. (With copper powder instead of the copper(I) salt the reaction is called the **Gattermann** reaction.)

**(b) Reimer-Tiemann reaction.** Phenol is heated with **chloroform and aqueous/alcoholic alkali**, and a **formyl group enters ortho to the hydroxyl**, giving salicylaldehyde:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> o-HOC6H4CHO + 3KCl + 2H2O}$$

The reactive species is **dichlorocarbene, $\ce{:CCl2}$**, generated by the action of hydroxide on chloroform; the strongly activated ring is attacked by this electrophile. Salicylaldehyde is the starting material for many coumarin and aspirin-type syntheses. With carbon tetrachloride instead of chloroform the product is salicylic acid.

**(c) Finkelstein reaction.** An alkyl chloride or bromide is refluxed with **sodium iodide in dry acetone**, giving the alkyl iodide:

$$\ce{R-Cl + NaI ->[\text{dry acetone}] R-I + NaCl v}$$

The driving force is solubility: NaI dissolves in acetone but NaCl and NaBr do not, so the precipitation of the sodium halide pulls the equilibrium to the right. It is an S$_N$2 substitution and the standard preparation of alkyl iodides (which are otherwise made from red phosphorus and iodine).
